newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin sees no new huge spending items.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin sees no new huge spending items.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Tuesday the ruling Liberal Party's election platform would not include huge new spending initiatives beyond a health care announcement made on Monday.

"What I am saying is that the (health care) announcement made by the prime minister yesterday in terms of dollars is by far the most important single announcement that will be made (in the Liberal campaign)," Martin told a news conference organized by the Canadian Broadcasting Corp.

Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Monday that the Liberal government, if re-elected on June 2, would not proceed with planned cuts to health care and social transfer payments to the provinces, starting with the next fiscal year.

Martin told reporters in Montreal: "Let me be very clear we are going to eliminate the deficit. We are going to get the debt to GDP ratio on a a downward trend. We are going to maintain inflation low and we are going to create jobs."
He said that economists have predicted Canada's economy would be strong over the next two years, "and we are not going to let that be frittered away."

Martin said he was not worried about the weakening in the Canadian dollar on Monday and Tuesday after the prime minister's announcement of the increased cash transfer to the provinces for health care.
"No. As you know, the international markets are very volatile," Martin said.
"You should not forget that the Canadian dollar is stronger compared with the (Japanese) yen and (German) mark and other currencies," he said.
Martin also repeated his opposition to tax cuts in the near term, something proposed by Conservative leader Jean Charest and Reform Party leader Preston Manning.

"I want to lower taxes. We will lower the taxes. But all of the economists are unanimous in saying that a reduction of taxes right now, paid for by another substantial cut in (government) programs, as advocated by Jean Charest and Preston Manning, would hurt enormously the creation of jobs," Martin said.
Martin said taxes would be reduced once the federal government deficit was eliminated.
